title: How do we know when we're looking at expert teaching?
author: Paul Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva
summary: In the third post of a series on becoming an expert teacher, Paul Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva ask how expertise in teaching can be recognised when, unlike tennis or chess, it lacks clear objective metrics. They argue that this gap pushes people toward easily visible surface features such as a lively room, a charismatic teacher, polished routines or years of experience, none of which is a real measure of expertise. Drawing on Robert Coe's warnings about poor proxies for learning and Daniel Willingham's line that memory is the residue of thought, they contend that visible engagement says little about what is happening in students' heads. The better yardstick, imperfect though it is, is student progress over time, which they link to the teacher factors that matter most, such as feedback, instructional quality, explicit instruction and mastery learning. They add an equity argument, that low-achieving students gain most from effective teachers and lose most from ineffective ones, and note that observing teaching is itself a trained skill, comparable to reading a CT scan.
points: Charisma, experience and a busy, engaged-looking classroom are poor indicators of expertise, because experience only creates the opportunity for expertise and visible engagement can coexist with little learning.
The post proposes judging teaching by what students learn, retain and can apply over time, accepting that this measure is messy but better than appearances.
Teacher effects accumulate across years, and the equity stakes are high because weaker students depend most on strong teaching.
Observation is a learned skill, so untrained observers will default to noise levels, polish and busyness rather than the quality of explanations and handling of misconceptions.
Schools that keep rewarding surface features will keep training people to notice the wrong things.
quotes: Education has a long history of rewarding appearances, even when those appearances tell us very little about whether students are actually learning. But what you’re seeing could be (is?) an educational illusion.
A teacher can spend years in the classroom and still plateau, repeating familiar habits rather than refining them. They can also repeat and refine things that don’t work.
What really matters is that students are thinking hard about the right things and that they are cognitively engaged (which can be very quiet and solitary).
Daniel Willingham wrote, “Memory is the residue of thought.” Students remember what they think about. If what they remember is the fun and not the content, then we have a problem.
This means that expertise isn’t merely a professional nicety; it’s one of the most powerful levers we have to reduce educational inequities.

If you don’t know what to look for, you’ll be drawn to easily visible things like performance, polish, noise levels, confidence, or general busyness. If you do know, your attention shifts toward student thinking, the quality of explanations, the handling of misconceptions, the design of tasks, and the evidence of learning accumulating over time.
The real sign of expertise lies less in the visible performance of the teacher than in the progress of the learner.
